questions.stem: Employees will enter an 8-foot-deep trench in soil that is not stable rock. What is required before entry?
options: No protection if the crew will remain less than 30 minutes
Only a warning sign at the trench edge
A compliant protective system selected for the soil and conditions
Protection only after the first sign of soil movement
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Trenches 5 feet or deeper require a protective system unless the excavation is entirely in stable rock.
incorrectOptionExplanations: OSHA does not create a short-duration exemption from cave-in protection.
A sign does not protect employees from a collapse.
Waiting for visible movement is too late and does not meet the preventive requirement.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 25, excavation protective systems, pp. 567-572; OSHA trenching requirements

questions.stem: Where should excavated spoil generally be placed relative to the edge of a trench?
options: Directly at the edge to reduce hauling
At least 6 inches from the edge
Inside the trench beside the access ladder
At least 2 feet from the edge or otherwise retained
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Keeping spoil at least 2 feet back reduces surcharge and material-fall hazards unless an effective retaining method is used.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Placing spoil at the edge adds surcharge load and creates falling-object hazards.
Six inches does not provide the required separation.
Spoil inside the trench obstructs egress and exposes workers to falling material.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 25, excavation safety, pp. 567-572; OSHA 1926.651(j)

questions.stem: Workers are in a trench 5 feet deep. How should a ladder or other safe egress be located?
options: So no worker must travel more than 25 feet laterally
One ladder at either end regardless of trench length
Only within 100 feet of the crew
Egress is optional when a competent person is present
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: For trenches 4 feet or deeper, safe egress must be located so employees travel no more than 25 feet laterally.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Long trenches require access points based on worker travel distance, not simply at the ends.
A 100-foot travel distance exceeds the OSHA requirement.
Competent-person oversight does not replace required safe access and egress.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 25, safe entry and exit, p. 571; OSHA 1926.651(c)(2)

questions.stem: Heavy rain occurs overnight at an active excavation. What must happen before employees reenter?
options: The previous day inspection remains valid
A competent person must inspect the excavation and protective system for changed hazards
Only the equipment operator must approve entry
Entry may resume after water is pumped out without further review
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Excavations require competent-person inspections daily and after events such as rainstorms that could increase hazards.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Changing weather can alter soil stability, water conditions, and protective-system performance.
The equipment operator may provide information but does not automatically fulfill the competent-person role.
Removing water does not address all possible changes caused by the rain.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 25, excavation inspections, pp. 567-572; OSHA trenching guidance

questions.stem: Using a 1.5 horizontal to 1 vertical slope for an 8-foot-deep Type C excavation, how far must the slope extend horizontally on each side?
options: 5.3 feet
8 feet
12 feet
16 feet
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Horizontal distance = 1.5*8 feet = 12 feet on each side.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This divides depth by 1.5 instead of multiplying by the horizontal ratio.
This assumes a 1:1 slope.
This assumes a 2:1 slope rather than the stated ratio.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 25, soil classifications and sloping, pp. 569-571

questions.stem: A construction employee works beside an unprotected edge 9 feet above a lower level. Which statement is correct?
options: Protection is not required until 10 feet
A warning sign alone always satisfies the requirement
Protection is required only if the employee carries materials
A compliant fall-protection system is required
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: At 6 feet or more above a lower level, employees at unprotected sides and edges generally require guardrails, safety nets, or personal fall arrest.
incorrectOptionExplanations: The general construction threshold for an unprotected side or edge is 6 feet, not 10 feet.
A warning sign alone is not the general control required for this exposure.
Fall-protection requirements do not depend on whether materials are being carried.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 25, fall protection in construction, pp. 583-590; OSHA 1926.501

questions.stem: A supported scaffold is expected to carry a maximum intended load of 1,200 pounds, excluding its own weight. What minimum load capacity must the components generally support without failure?
options: 4,800 pounds plus the scaffold own weight
1,200 pounds total
2,400 pounds plus the scaffold own weight
7,200 pounds plus the scaffold own weight
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Scaffold components generally must support their own weight and at least four times the maximum intended load.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Supporting only the intended load does not provide the required capacity factor.
This applies a factor of two instead of four.
A factor of six applies to certain suspension ropes, not the general scaffold component rule.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)

questions.stem: An employee works on a supported scaffold platform 13 feet above a lower level. What protection is generally required?
options: No protection because the scaffold is below 15 feet
A guardrail system, personal fall-arrest system, or the required combination for the scaffold type
Only a controlled-access-zone sign
A body belt used as a fall-arrest device
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Employees on scaffolds more than 10 feet above a lower level require fall protection appropriate to the scaffold type.
incorrectOptionExplanations: The scaffold fall-protection threshold is more than 10 feet above a lower level.
A sign does not provide the fall protection required for scaffold work.
Body belts are not permitted as personal fall-arrest systems.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 25, scaffold fall hazards, pp. 580-583; OSHA 1926.451(g)

questions.stem: Temporary 120-volt receptacles are used on a construction site. Which program approach is acceptable for employee protection?
options: Use extension cords without grounding if inspected visually
Rely only on circuit breakers at the service panel
Use GFCIs or an assured equipment grounding conductor program that meets the standard
Allow each employee to decide whether protection is needed
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Construction rules allow GFCI protection or a compliant assured equipment grounding conductor program for covered receptacles.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Visual inspection does not replace required ground-fault or grounding-conductor protection.
A standard overcurrent device may not respond quickly enough to low-level ground-fault current.
Protection is an employer program requirement, not an individual preference.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 25, electrical safety in construction, pp. 572-578; OSHA construction electrical requirements

questions.stem: A crane will operate near a 34.5 kV overhead power line. Unless the line is deenergized and grounded or other compliant protections are used, what minimum clearance is generally required?
options: 3 feet
6 feet
20 feet
10 feet
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: For lines up to 50 kV, the commonly applied minimum clearance is 10 feet unless a compliant alternative is established.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Three feet is not the general crane clearance for this voltage.
Six feet is associated with some fall-protection thresholds, not overhead-line clearance.
Twenty feet may be used as a planning trigger in some crane procedures, but the stated general minimum for up to 50 kV is 10 feet.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 25, cranes and electrical hazards, pp. 572-590; OSHA construction power-line rules

questions.stem: Welding will occur near combustible packaging that cannot be moved beyond the exposure area. What is the best control before work begins?
options: Shield or cover the combustibles and provide an appropriate fire watch with extinguishing capability
Begin work if the welder has flame-resistant clothing
Wet only the welding leads
Rely on the building alarm system as the primary control
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Hot-work controls should remove or protect combustibles and provide a fire watch when conditions warrant.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Welder PPE does not control ignition of nearby combustible material.
Wetting leads does not protect exposed combustibles and may create electrical hazards.
Detection and alarm do not replace ignition prevention and immediate fire-watch response.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 25, welding, cutting, brazing, and fire prevention, pp. 592-597

questions.stem: Compressed air is proposed for cleaning metal chips from a workbench. Which condition is required for permissible cleaning use?
options: Any pressure if the nozzle is held more than 12 inches away
Pressure below 30 psi with effective chip guarding and personal protection
Up to 100 psi when safety glasses are worn
No pressure limit when cleaning is brief
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: OSHA permits compressed air for cleaning only when reduced below 30 psi and used with effective chip guarding and PPE.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Distance from the nozzle does not replace the pressure and guarding requirements.
Safety glasses alone do not permit 100 psi cleaning.
Short duration does not remove the requirement to control pressure and flying chips.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 25, compressed air systems, pp. 601-602; OSHA 1926.302(b)(4)

questions.stem: A bench grinder has an intact wheel but the work rest is far from the wheel, allowing the workpiece to become trapped. What is the best correction?
options: Remove the work rest to provide more room
Use heavier gloves and keep the existing gap
Adjust the work rest to the required close clearance and inspect the guard system before use
Increase wheel speed so the workpiece cannot lodge
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Properly adjusted rests and guards prevent the workpiece from being caught between the rest and wheel.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Removing the rest increases the trapping and loss-of-control hazard.
Gloves do not correct the mechanical nip point and may add entanglement risk.
Higher speed increases energy and does not eliminate the excessive gap.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 25, abrasive grinders and hand/power tools, pp. 597-601

questions.stem: A trench more than 4 feet deep is opened near a former fuel line. What should occur before employees enter?
options: Assume natural ventilation makes testing unnecessary
Rely on odor as the only indicator
Enter briefly first and test only if symptoms occur
Test for oxygen deficiency and hazardous atmospheres and provide controls as indicated
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Where a hazardous atmosphere could reasonably exist in an excavation over 4 feet deep, testing is required before entry.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Depth, location, and potential contamination create a foreseeable atmospheric hazard requiring evaluation.
Odor is unreliable and may be absent, masked, or cause olfactory fatigue.
Using employees as detectors exposes them before conditions are known.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 25, excavation hazards, pp. 567-572; OSHA trenching guidance

questions.stem: Workers must pass beneath a scaffold where tools are used above. Which control combination is strongest?
options: Prevent objects from falling with toe boards, screens, or tool restraint and control access below
Require hard hats only
Post a warning sign and leave the walkway open
Ask upper-level workers to shout before moving tools
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Source control and exclusion of the drop zone are stronger than relying only on personal protective equipment.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Hard hats reduce injury severity but do not prevent objects from falling.
A sign alone does not control the falling-object source or exposure area.
Verbal warnings are unreliable and do not provide continuous protection.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 25, scaffold and falling-object protection, pp. 580-584
